title: Do you make your AI agents write tests for gameplay code, or do you just playtest everything yourself?
author: shanebrumback
selftext:
I keep seeing people ship AI-built games with hundreds of automated tests, and others who never write one and just play the build after every change. I'm somewhere in the middle and trying to figure out where tests actually pay off when an agent writes most of the code.

Where tests seem worth it to me:
- \*\*Rules and math:\*\* damage, ammo, cooldowns, score, respawn timers. Easy to test, and agents break them quietly when they touch nearby code.
- \*\*Asset contracts:\*\* does the character file still have the bones and animation names the code expects? One check catches a lot of silent breakage.
- \*\*Multiplayer state:\*\* given these inputs, do two clients end up in the same state?

Where I still just play it:
- Game feel: camera, recoil, movement weight.
- Anything visual. An agent can read a screenshot, but it doesn't tell you the game is fun.

Questions for people building with AI:
1. Do you ask the agent to write tests with every feature, or add them only after something breaks twice?
2. Has an agent ever "fixed" a failing test by changing the test instead of the code? How do you stop that?
3. Do you run headless playthroughs or bot matches as a test?
4. Is it worth it for a small solo game, or only once several agents are working at once?

Disclosure: I write about Three.js + AI on my own site. Not linking it here, I'm just interested in how others handle this.

comments.author: Useful_Use_6170
comments.body: I have my agent simulate  hours okayed , days , weeks and specific behavior for balancing

comments.author: Glittering-Sleep7983
comments.body: It's always fascinating to me reading posts like this and makes me wonder what AI models everyone else is using. I have to fight Opus, Fable, and Astra tooth and nail to stop writing so many unit tests and full game simulation tests.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body: Mine takes a bazillion screenshots to verify functionality. Every week or so I have to tell it to do a mass culling of tests and screenshot protocols

replies.author: ZymzAlchemy
replies.body:
They do seem to take alot of screenshots, mine likes to make videos also occasionally so that's a good time. lol

When I got into this I figured it would be a no-brainer because I've been doing this for 40+ years but it's like working with a brand new guy who just got out of college, fresh from his coding classes and has no clue how to do real world software development. 

You have to treat them like simpletons and guardrail them tightly.

replies.author: Disastrous-Gain5870
replies.body: Because they’ve never been trained to game dev. I think once they take more training data from actual game devs, they’ll get much more efficient. In 6 months I think the difference will be astronomical.

replies.author: ZymzAlchemy
replies.body:
Edit your 'AGENTS.md' and add something like - "Write and execute only the minimum tests strictly required to verify your immediate changes; do not generate or run extraneous, speculative, or preventative tests."

I also have in there a directive to run regression testing to ensure the agent isn't trampling all over verified and working code segments.

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body:
Min or max are fairly easy criteria for AI to understand, but IMO a specific testing standard is better.  

Something that is very clear about exactly when what kind of test is required, and exactly when to run it.

replies.author: ZymzAlchemy
replies.body:
Fair point. Replace the vague 'minimum' with a hard standard: 

*'Write exactly one unit test per new or modified function, and run the full regression suite only at the end of each phase. Do not write edge-case or preventative tests.'*

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body: Totally. Could be a table or list, too.

replies.author: forgingtheflow
replies.body: I had to get my code session to review token usage a couple of times. It reduced usage down to 30% now, with hopefully similar outcomes. It even lets me know how much each task/slice will use of my weekly usage so we can plan what it can do and pre-empt when to stop building so I have usage left for other things.

comments.author: ZymzAlchemy
comments.body: Both. The agent creates tests it needs to verify and test the code it writes, including headed IDE runs. After, a human play test is the only way to be certain as the AI likes to pad the tests or isolate them in a 'test context' which omits the variable of real player input/recaction/response.

comments.author: jivenossauro
comments.body:
1 - I ask him to make less tests sometimes
2 - No
3 - I play from time to time and try out whatever new thing is made.
4 - you can have several agents working at once in a small solo game. It's worth it for everything

comments.author: forgingtheflow
comments.body:
I’m building two games, one is nearly completed. I’m trying to get playtesters to provide feedback etc. this first game I’ve probably started a new game easily several hundred times over the last 6 months, easily. For 75% of my test I start from the beginning and would record massive blocks of text with changes and fixes per session, then exit and paste what i wrote, wait for it to be done, then test again. I probably spent hundreds of hours not making it past the first 30 minutes of gameplay. 

My second game, I’ve been working on for over a month, 3 weeks of planning with Claude, so no code building. Created a massive handover doc and Claude code has been building it non stop for about 2 weeks now, I haven’t even loaded it, but I have watched it play the game and test, so that’s been interesting. Once it’s built, I’ll get my hands dirty and test it. 

This method for the second game has allowed me to keep working on the first game

replies.author: Sbrazen77
replies.body:
I’m curious, when you say it’s been building nonstop for two weeks are you just letting it have unlimited tokens to play with? Or do you have it stop and create checkpoints when usage is close to cap.

If it’s the first how many tokens are you at after 2 weeks 👀

replies.author: forgingtheflow
replies.body:
Sure, these are some stats from Claude - No Safe Orbit is the name of the game FYI, it mentions Milestone plans M1 - M7, in total there are 12 Milestones and I believe I have one left for the coding session to build. - Then, hopefully, hopefully I can finally test out the game my self. 



Here’s the whole-project count. It’s from every Claude Code session on No Safe Orbit, worktrees included, 5–18 October.

About 10.6 billion tokens, over roughly 34,000 model calls.

The early days ran 1–2 billion a day. The peak was 2.0 billion on 6 October, during M1–M3.

Since the lean workflow (16 October on) it has been about 1.4 billion over three days. That covers Runs A–E, Run D and the start of M12a.

The handover to the coding session was the project’s first commit, on 5 October 2026, labelled “docs, data, Python reference sim and golden runs”. It held **123 files, about 7 MB**, and about **230,000 words** of written documents, roughly 460 pages:

|Part|Files|Size|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Current design documents|17|about 82,000 words (around 165 pages)|
|Earlier design versions and test histories, kept for reference|25|about 102,000 words|
|Art handovers for the modelling sessions|6|about 32,000 words|
|Coding instructions, architecture, parity rules, glossary, UI port guide|12|about 9,000 words|
|Milestone plans, M0 to M7|9|about 4,900 words|
|Game data (economy world, ships, equipment and so on)|12|3.5 MB|
|Python reference sim, plus its golden runs|36|2.2 MB|

replies.author: Sbrazen77
replies.body:
Whew over 10 billion! 

Thanks for the insight

replies.author: forgingtheflow
replies.body: The handover doc was also surprising. I was hammering my ideas into Claude, then getting it to audit and find gaps etc, etc. It would disappear for hours running simulations and report back on what we added. So I had expected the coding session to be pretty quick because the blue print was all there. During the build the coding session had approx 200-300 questions it came up with, so as each slice was done I’d take the questions back to the planning session and we’d go through them. Then I’d hand the answer back and it would integrate them.

replies.author: Disastrous-Gain5870
replies.body: Interesting concept. I find it much easier to just implement something, test myself, and then fix whatever needs fixing. I can play my game for hours now if I want to without any bugs.

comments.author: Valentinevandal1986
comments.body: I basically give it a benchmark of what I deem an acceptable result and get it to work until it hits it. I’ve read its transcriptions while it’s working and it’ll say “tested but that failed to meet quality standards, rethinking my approach “

comments.author: Time_Cat_5212
comments.body:
When you say agents, what specifically do you mean?

I think I'd be way more rigorous about tests (and write them on a spike) if I had persistent agents running on a project. 

If I'm working directly with an agentic coding tool, I'd probably have tests cover a smaller surface area.

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: They write the tests themselves. You have to tell them to not test balance just make sure stuff works.

comments.author: CordusPorf
comments.body: Mine tend to write things in a deterministic way so that often time gameplay tests can be automated headlesly.

comments.author: MrShaitan
comments.body: I've done at least 200k matches for my game in simulation, using ChatGPT, it was maxing out a chat every 10 hours or so. I don't have any animations yet, so the simulated battles got the balance close enough, once I have animations and assets I'll do actual testing, but I think I was able to burn through a lot of the trial and error pretty fast through simulations.

comments.author: nephilimOokami
comments.body: Using godot, I built a playwright like framework for it to let me automate as much as possible, will open source this once i have it working as i wanted; also, built it with an mcp, so agents could test and write specs as well, so, basically, i test everything, visual taste and "workflows" still a thing only I judge over

comments.author: No_Entrepreneur6548
comments.body:
The issue today is the tests self validate the ais assumption of what that rule or outcome should be not what feels right. With opus I’ve worked on a pretty complex simulation of Wild West town. There are well over 350 buildings and so many events. While the tests “pass” and there are a ton of tests…. The difficulty is in balancing the complex engines to make the game feel fun. This has taken as long as building assets. Dealing with Performance issues and playtesting other aspects. 

You need to make sure you have some quick debug mode that you can dump variables and say “this is wrong or does not feel right because”. What I’ve done is an in game bug reporter. Any time there is an issue you press a button and it dumps the variables into a file. Then the ai can recreate it and help tweak it. 

The agents have always built headless tests with out me prompting. But again they validate their assumptions and you have to point out explicitly where they’re wrong because they’re looking for something more narrow. Sometimes I’m sitting there watching all these screen shots and other details pop up and am like “this guy has no head”. But since that’s not what it’s looking for in its context it doesn’t matter.

comments.author: AsnIsCrazyToo
comments.body: AI writes code ,tests code and fix bugs ...tests,fix, until finish it.

comments.author: Bonelessgummybear
comments.body: Having some test bots are useful. You can quickly see if changes affect balance. You need to playtest too but the bots are nice for minor balance patches and instant testing instead of replaying constantly

comments.author: Deelook
comments.body: What I did is to separate session from the code and had my [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) says it can't touch anything in /tests without asking first. I also check the git diff before accepting. If a test file changed in a feature commit, that's a red flag

comments.author: Disastrous-Gain5870
comments.body: Both, but most of the testing is done by me, because I’m a gamer, and I want my game to feel fluid and be fun. The people who leave EVERYTHING up to AI aren’t gamers.
